title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New G

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'up to 5× on manipulation tasks' but Table 1 shows Arm Binpick Hard improves 4.7×, Arm Push Easy 2.0×, and Arm Push Hard 2.1×. The only manipulation task reaching 5× is Arm Binpick Hard at 4.7×, which rounds to 5× but the abstract says 'up to 5×' suggesting at least one task reaches or exceeds 5×, which is not supported by the data.

The abstract claims 'more than 20× in half of the environments' but Table 1 shows only 4 out of 10 environments exceed 20×: Ant U4-Maze (20×), Ant U5-Maze (50×), Humanoid (42×), Humanoid U-Maze (40×), and Humanoid Big Maze (600×). That's 5 out of 10, which is exactly half, not 'more than 20× in half'. The phrasing suggests more than half achieve 20×, which is misleading.

The text in Section 4.2 states 'over $20\times$ gains in long-horizon maze tasks such as Ant U4-Maze and Ant U5-Maze' but Table 1 shows Ant U4-Maze has exactly 20× improvement (11.4 to 230), not 'over 20×'. Only Ant U5-Maze clearly exceeds 20× at 50×.

Section 4.2 states 'Scaling CRL leads to substantial performance improvements, outperforming all other baselines in 8 out of 10 tasks' but the caption for Figure 12 says 'Scaled CRL (ours) outperforms baselines... in 8 out of 10 environments.' However, the text also states 'The only exception is SAC on the Humanoid Maze environments' which would be 2 exceptions (Humanoid U-Maze and Humanoid Big Maze), making it 8 out of 10, which is consistent. But the figure shows SAC performing better on both Humanoid maze tasks, confirming 8/10.

The text states 'Figure 7 shows only marginal or inconsistent improvements from increasing batch size' but also claims 'larger networks can effectively leverage batch size scaling to achieve further improvements.' These statements appear contradictory - if the improvements are marginal/inconsistent, then the networks are not effectively leveraging batch size scaling.

The text states 'for the 1024-layer networks, we observed the actor loss exploding at the onset of training, so we maintained the actor depth at 512 while using 1024-layer networks only for the two critic encoders.' This contradicts the paper's main claim about scaling depth uniformly - the 1024-layer result is not actually a 1024-layer network but a mixed 512/1024 architecture, making the comparison inconsistent with other depth experiments.

Figure 2 states 'We define network depth as the number of residual blocks N, each containing 4 Dense layers, so the effective number of layers is 4N. To avoid confusion, experimental depths (4, 8, 16, etc.) refer explicitly to the total number of Dense layers.' However, this creates confusion because a 'depth 4' network would have 1 residual block, but the architecture shows multiple components. The definition is internally inconsistent about whether depth refers to total layers or residual blocks.

Table 1 reports Humanoid Big Maze improvement as '600×' (from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 40 ± 21). However, 40/0.06 = 666×, not 600×. While this could be rounding, the large uncertainty (±0.04 on 0.06 means the baseline could be 0.02-0.10) makes the 600× claim potentially misleading - the improvement could range from 400× to 2000× depending on the actual baseline value.

The section claims 'Emergent Policies Through Depth' and describes 'emergent behaviors' but then states 'While we observed some anecdotal differences in learned policies at varying depths, especially in humanoid tasks, we do not find conclusive quantitative evidence that these behaviors represent consistent qualitative leaps.' This admission contradicts the section title and undermines the claim of emergence, yet the paper continues to use 'emergent' language throughout.

Section 4.4 discusses 'The (CRL) Algorithm is Key' and claims CRL enables depth scaling, but Section 4.6 states 'We found little evidence that increasing the network depth of CRL improves performance in this offline setting' and 'baseline depth-4 networks often had the highest success.' This suggests the algorithm is NOT the key factor, but rather the online setting, contradicting the section 4.4 claim.

Figure 13 shows tables with numerical values for different algorithms at different depths. For SAC on Humanoid, the values are listed as 'Depth 4 8 16 32 64; Value 330 358 256 282 348' but these values show depth 16 (256) performing worse than depth 4 (330), which contradicts the claim that depth scaling doesn't help - it actually hurts. However, the figure caption states 'Depth scaling yields limited gains' when the data shows negative effects, which is understating the problem.

The text states 'For Humanoid, aggressive scaling of both actor and critic networks confers the highest gains, with coordinated depth increases resulting in an average 30% improvement over critic-only or actor-only scaling across tasks.' However, Figure 6 shows specific numerical values that don't clearly support a '30% improvement' claim - the values need to be verified against this specific percentage claim.
